title: High Energy-efficiency and Low latency In-Memory Computing using Analog Accumulator and In-Memory ADC with shared References
problem: In-memory computing array ADCs require high area overhead for data conversion; traditional approaches sacrifice linearity and energy efficiency.
motivation: In-memory analog-to-digital conversion consumes large area; efficient shared-reference designs can drastically reduce overhead while maintaining signal integrity.
method: The system builds a 256-by-128 array of dual-8T SRAM bitcells (memory cells containing 8 transistors each, grouped in pairs) that store three-level weights rather than binary, keeping read and write operations separate for better efficiency. To handle multi-bit inputs, it splits them into single bits (a process called bit-slicing) and combines them using a charge-sharing binary weighted accumulator—a circuit where electrical charge flows between weighted components to add values more efficiently than traditional circuits. A reading technique called Read WWL Under Drive lowers the electrical current during reading, which reduces current variation and noise.
key_novelty: The key innovation is sharing reference signals across a reconfigurable in-memory converter (ADC), which reduces area overhead by 9 times while achieving 1146 trillion operations per watt.
contributions: Reconfigurable in-memory ADC with shared references reducing area overhead by 9x (3% vs traditional)
Charge-sharing binary weighted accumulator (CHA) for low-latency multi-bit handling
Bit-slicing approach improving throughput by 1.9x and linearity by 23x vs pulse-width modulation
1146 TOPS/W and 27 TOPS/mm^2 energy and area efficiency with <1% accuracy loss on vision/graph tasks
baselines: Traditional in-memory ADC with non-shared references
limitations: Evaluation limited to smaller models (MLP/VGG-8/GCN); scalability to larger CNNs not discussed.
primary_theme: Shared-reference in-memory ADC for efficient analog compute arrays
